claim: Abstract representations organize complex action sequences in terms of subplans (chunks) and sequential positions.
source: Despite strong theoretical reasons for assuming that abstract representations organize complex action sequences in terms of subplans (chunks) and sequential positions, we lack methods to directly track such content-independent, hierarchical representations in humans.
evidence: This is a theoretical assumption stated in the abstract that frames the research question.

claim: Theta and alpha-band activity coded basic elements and abstract control representations across three experiments.
source: Across three experiments, the theta and alpha-band activity coded basic elements and abstract control representations, in particular, the ordinal position of basic elements, but also the identity and position of chunks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from three experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Theta and alpha-band activity coded the ordinal position of basic elements.
source: Across three experiments, the theta and alpha-band activity coded basic elements and abstract control representations, in particular, the ordinal position of basic elements, but also the identity and position of chunks.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data.

claim: Theta and alpha-band activity coded the identity and position of chunks.
source: Across three experiments, the theta and alpha-band activity coded basic elements and abstract control representations, in particular, the ordinal position of basic elements, but also the identity and position of chunks.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data.

claim: Robust representation of higher level chunk identity information was only found in individuals with above-median working memory capacity.
source: Further, a robust representation of higher level, chunk identity information was only found in individuals with above-median working memory capacity, potentially providing a neural-level explanation for working-memory differences in sequential performance.
evidence: This is a finding from individual differences analysis in the experiments.

claim: The finding that chunk identity information is only robust in high-WM individuals potentially provides a neural-level explanation for working-memory differences in sequential performance.
source: Further, a robust representation of higher level, chunk identity information was only found in individuals with above-median working memory capacity, potentially providing a neural-level explanation for working-memory differences in sequential performance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Decoding oscillatory activity can track how the cognitive system traverses through the states of a hierarchical control structure.
source: Our results suggest that by decoding oscillatory activity we can track how the cognitive system traverses through the states of a hierarchical control structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Many theorists believe that sequential skills are achieved through a set of abstract, content-independent control representations that code the position of basic elements within shorter subsequences (i.e. chunks) or the position of chunks within a hierarchically organized plan.
source: Following Lashley (1951), many theorists believe that such sequential skills are achieved through a set of abstract, content-independent control representations that code the position of basic elements within shorter subsequences (i.e. chunks) or the position of chunks within a hierarchically organized plan (Dehaene et al., 2015; MacKay, 2012; Rosenbaum et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work in the field.

claim: Hierarchical control representations have been proposed as the hallmark of complex, flexible behavior in humans, including motor or action control.
source: Hierarchical control representations have been proposed as the hallmark of complex, flexible behavior in humans, including motor or action control (Collard and Povel, 1982; Cooper and Shallice, 2006; Rosenbaum et al., 1983; Schneider and Logan, 2006), language (Fitch and Martins, 2014), or problem solving (Carpenter et al., 1990; Miller et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Hierarchical control representations have been proposed as the hallmark of complex, flexible behavior in humans, including language.
source: Hierarchical control representations have been proposed as the hallmark of complex, flexible behavior in humans, including motor or action control (Collard and Povel, 1982; Cooper and Shallice, 2006; Rosenbaum et al., 1983; Schneider and Logan, 2006), language (Fitch and Martins, 2014), or problem solving (Carpenter et al., 1990; Miller et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Hierarchical control representations have been proposed as the hallmark of complex, flexible behavior in humans, including problem solving.
source: Hierarchical control representations have been proposed as the hallmark of complex, flexible behavior in humans, including motor or action control (Collard and Povel, 1982; Cooper and Shallice, 2006; Rosenbaum et al., 1983; Schneider and Logan, 2006), language (Fitch and Martins, 2014), or problem solving (Carpenter et al., 1990; Miller et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Serial order can be established through more parsimonious mechanisms based on learning associative links between consecutive elements (chaining), without having to assume content-independent representations.
source: However, in principle, serial order can also be established through more parsimonious mechanisms based on learning associtive links between between consecutive elements (often referred to as 'chaining'), without having to assume content-independent representations (Botvinick and Plaut, 2004; Davachi and DuBrow, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: The abstract nature of serial-order control representations has made it difficult to provide direct evidence for their existence, to distinguish them from chaining-based representations, or to characterize their functional properties.
source: Empirically, it is exactly the abstract nature of serial-order control representations that has made it difficult to provide direct evidence for their existence, to distinguish them from chaining-based representations, or to characterize their functional properties.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on established knowledge.

claim: Flexibly generated and explicitly instructed sequential behavior is achieved through hierarchical control representations.
source: The current work tests the general hypothesis that flexibly generated and explicitly instructed, sequential behavior is achieved through hierarchical control representations and that these representations are reflected in the pattern of rhythmic EEG (electroencephalogram) activity.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis being tested in the study.

claim: Hierarchical control representations are reflected in the pattern of rhythmic EEG activity.
source: The current work tests the general hypothesis that flexibly generated and explicitly instructed, sequential behavior is achieved through hierarchical control representations and that these representations are reflected in the pattern of rhythmic EEG (electroencephalogram) activity.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis being tested in the study.

claim: Dynamic, large-scale neural communication can be achieved through frequency-specific, rhythmic activity that coordinates local and global cellular assemblies.
source: A number of results suggest that such dynamic, large-scale neural communication can be achieved through frequency-specific, rhythmic activity that coordinates local and global cellular assemblies (Buzsaki, 2006; Fries, 2005; Helfrich and Knight, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The power of cortical oscillations in the theta band (4 to 7 Hz) increases as a function of serial-order processing demands.
source: For example, the power of cortical oscillations in the theta band (4 to 7 Hz) increases as a function of serial-order processing demands (Gevins et al., 1997; Jensen and Lisman, 2005; Jensen and Tesche, 2002; Roberts et al., 2013; Sauseng et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Short-term memory of the order of serially presented visual objects was associated with increased frontal theta-band power.
source: Specifically, Hsieh et al. (2011) reported that short-term memory of the order of serially presented visual objects was associated with increased frontal theta-band power.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific prior study.

claim: The memory of items themselves was related to changes in posterior alpha power (8 to 12 Hz).
source: In contrast, the memory of the items themselves was related to changes in posterior alpha power (8 to 12 Hz, e.g. Foster et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Both the content and the serial order of a sequence are represented in oscillatory activity.
source: Combined, these results indicate that both the content and the serial order of a sequence are represented in oscillatory activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited prior research.

claim: Activity in the alpha-band may code for basic elements and in the theta-band for how elements are ordered.
source: Furthermore, these results provide some evidence that activity in the alpha-band may code for basic elements and in the theta-band for how elements are ordered.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited prior research.

claim: Goal-relevant properties induce large-scale neural responses that are specific to the contents of representations.
source: Second, goal-relevant properties induce large-scale neural responses that are specific to the contents of representations (Barak et al., 2010; Stokes et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neural response profiles can be decoded with time-resolved, multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) from the pattern of spectral-temporal profile of EEG or MEG activity.
source: These neural response profiles in turn can be decoded with time-resolved, multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) from the pattern of spectral-temporal profile of EEG or MEG activity (Foster et al., 2016; Fukuda et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: More abstract information, such as decision confidence or semantic categories can be decoded from the pattern of activity distributed over the scalp.
source: While the majority of this research has focused on the representation of basic perceptual properties, there is also initial evidence that more abstract information, such as decision confidence (King et al., 2016) or semantic categories (Chan et al., 2011) can be decoded from the pattern of activity distributed over the scalp.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Abstract, serial-order control representations can be decoded from the EEG signal independently of the basic elements.
source: We test here the hypothesis that even abstract, serial-order control representations can be decoded from the EEG signal independently of the basic elements.
evidence: This is a hypothesis being tested in the study.

claim: Traditional models of hierarchical control are informed by the characteristic response time (RT) pattern during sequence production, with long RTs at chunk transitions and bursts of fast, within-chunk responses.
source: Traditional models of hierarchical control are informed by the characteristic response time (RT) pattern during sequence production, with long RTs at chunk transitions and bursts of fast, within-chunk responses (Collard and Povel, 1982; Rosenbaum et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Higher level, chunk representations may be needed only during chunk transitions, after which control is handed down to representations that code for the position and elements within chunks.
source: This pattern may indicate that higher level, chunk representations are needed only during chunk transitions, after which control is handed down to representations that code for the position and elements within chunks.
evidence: This is a theoretical possibility inferred from prior research patterns.

claim: Higher level codes may need to remain active while lower level representations are being used—in order to ward off interference from competing chunks, or to maintain the ability to navigate within the overall control structure once within-chunk processing has completed.
source: Alternatively, higher level codes may need to remain active while lower level representations are being used—in order to ward off interference from competing chunks, or to maintain the ability to navigate within the overall control structure once within-chunk processing has completed.
evidence: This is an alternative theoretical possibility.

claim: Initial evidence points to the importance of working memory (WM) capacity as one limiting factor during sequential performance, at least for longer sequences.
source: Initial evidence points to the importance of working memory (WM) capacity as one limiting factor during sequential performance, at least for longer sequences (Bo and Seidler, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: WM may limit the quality of representations in a uniform manner.
source: One possibility is that WM limits the quality of representations in a uniform manner.
evidence: This is a theoretical possibility being considered.

claim: If WM limits representations uniformly, decodability of all representations, no matter which type or level, is reduced for individuals with low WM capacity.
source: This would imply that decodability of all representations, no matter which type (i.e. content or structural), or on which level, is reduced for individuals with low WM capacity.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the theoretical possibility.

claim: The chunking of larger sequences into smaller subunits occurs precisely to protect representations from WM-related constraints.
source: Arguably, however, the chunking of larger sequences into smaller subunits occurs precisely to protect representations from WM-related constraints (Brady et al., 2009; Cowan, 1988; Oberauer, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Individual differences in sequential performance should be determined by the degree to which higher level representations can be maintained, while action selection is controlled by within-chunk representations.
source: Thus, based on this view, individual differences in sequential performance should be determined by the degree to which higher level representations can be maintained, while action selection is controlled by within-chunk representations.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on cited prior work.

claim: Low WM capacity selectively affects decodability of higher level representations of chunk identity and/or position, but does not affect lower level, within-chunk representations.
source: This would lead to the prediction that low WM capacity selectively affects decodability of higher level representations of chunk identity and/or position, but does not affect lower level, within-chunk representations.
evidence: This is a specific prediction derived from theoretical reasoning.

claim: There is evidence from studies using short-term memory tasks and fMRI neuroimaging for ordinal position codes in humans.
source: In humans, there is already some evidence from studies using short-term memory tasks and fMRI neuroimaging for ordinal position codes (Desrochers et al., 2015; Heusser et al., 2016; Kalm and Norris, 2014; Lehn et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It can be problematic to interpret position-specific information in most standard paradigms due to serial-position confounds.
source: However, as recently argued by Kalm and Norris (2017a), it can be problematic to interpret position-specific information in most standard paradigms.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior critical analysis.

claim: With the combination of short-term memory tasks and the low temporal resolution of fMRI, it is difficult to rule out serial-position confounds, such as sensory adaptation, temporal distance from a context change, or differences in processing load.
source: Specifically, with the combination of short-term memory tasks and the low temporal resolution of fMRI, it is difficult to rule out serial-position confounds, such as sensory adaptation, temporal distance from a context change (i.e. beginning of a probe period), or differences in processing load (i.e. higher retrieval demands or uncertainty at the start of a sequence or chunk).
evidence: This claim is based on cited prior critical analysis.

claim: Even if position codes can be validly decoded from fMRI signals, it is difficult to draw strong conclusions about the temporal dynamics between different serial-order control representations.
source: Further, even if position codes can be validly decoded from fMRI signals, it is difficult to draw strong conclusions about the temporal dynamics between different serial-order control representations.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of fMRI based on established knowledge.

claim: fMRI neuroimaging studies have yielded important insights about the neural basis of different levels within a hierarchical control structure.
source: Similarly, while fMRI neuroimaging studies have yielded important insights about the neural basis of different levels within a hierarchical control structure (Badre and D'Esposito, 2009; Farooqui et al., 2012; Koechlin and Summerfield, 2007), we know very little about when in the course of sequential performance, which control representations are active.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: We know very little about when in the course of sequential performance, which control representations are active.
source: Similarly, while fMRI neuroimaging studies have yielded important insights about the neural basis of different levels within a hierarchical control structure (Badre and D'Esposito, 2009; Farooqui et al., 2012; Koechlin and Summerfield, 2007), we know very little about when in the course of sequential performance, which control representations are active.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: By using EEG signals, we are in a better position to track the temporal dynamics of serial-order control codes than when relying on fMRI analyses.
source: By using EEG signals, we are in a better position to track the temporal dynamics of serial-order control codes than when relying on fMRI analyses.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the method used in the study.

claim: The experimental paradigm was designed to create a situation in which the use of content-independent control codes was particularly likely.
source: With our experimental paradigm, we tried to create a situation in which the use of content-independent control codes was particularly likely and that allowed us to minimize the serial-position confounds identified by Kalm and Norris (2017a).
evidence: This is a statement about the design rationale of the study.

claim: The experimental paradigm was designed to minimize the serial-position confounds identified by Kalm and Norris (2017a).
source: With our experimental paradigm, we tried to create a situation in which the use of content-independent control codes was particularly likely and that allowed us to minimize the serial-position confounds identified by Kalm and Norris (2017a).
evidence: This is a statement about the design rationale of the study.

claim: Participants were instructed to 'cycle through' a particular 9-element sequence (or six elements in Experiment 3) repeatedly within a block of trials.
source: In our procedure, participants were instructed to 'cycle through' a particular 9-element sequence (or six elements in Experiment 3) repeatedly within a block of trials (for a similar procedure using fMRI, see Desrochers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: In each block, a new sequence was instructed, but all sequences consisted of recombinations of the same, small set of three basic elements.
source: In each block, a new sequence was instructed, but all sequences consisted of recombinations of the same, small set of three basic elements (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The cycling-sequence paradigm provides very little opportunity for an associative chaining process to control sequential performance.
source: Such a situation provides very little opportunity for an associative chaining process to control sequential performance.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the experimental design.

claim: Previous work had provided strong behavioral evidence that within this paradigm, serial-order control is achieved through hierarchically organized, content-independent position codes.
source: In fact, previous work had provided strong behavioral evidence that within this paradigm, serial-order control is achieved through hierarchically organized, content-independent position codes (Mayr, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In Experiment 1, the chunk boundary effect in RTs was 14 ms (SD = 18).
source: For Experiment 1, which used the fixed-paced procedure, RTs showed a small, but reliable chunk boundary effect of 14 ms (SD = 18) in RTs, F(1,28) = 19.20, MSE = 622.47, p < 0.001
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 1, the chunk boundary effect in errors was 3.8% (SD = 4.3).
source: and a robust error effect of 3.8% (SD = 4.3), F(1,28) = 22.70, MSE < 0.01, p < 0.001.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, the chunk boundary effect in RTs was 5 ms (SD = 9.3).
source: For Experiment 2, where participants moved to the next trial only after indicating per key-press that they had retrieved the upcoming orientation, the chunking pattern in RTs, while still reliable was with 5 ms (SD = 9.3) was even smaller than in Experiment 1 for RTs, F(1,28) = 8.05, MSE = 168.79, p = 0.01
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, the chunk boundary effect in errors was 3.5% (SD = 4.9%).
source: but with 3.5% (SD = 4.9%) equally strong for errors, F(1,28) = 18.41, MSE < 0.01, p < 0.001.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was a very strong chunk-boundary effect of 372 ms (SD = 361) in the self-paced retrieval times.
source: There was a very strong chunk-boundary effect of 372 ms (SD = 361) in the self-paced retrieval times, F(1,28) = 35.43, MSE = 234826, p < 0.001.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data.

claim: The self-paced retrieval instruction was effective in removing an even larger share of the retrieval demands from the EEG-recorded preparation period.
source: Thus, overall the self-paced retrieval instruction was effective in removing an even larger share of the retrieval demands from the EEG-recorded preparation period.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The additional opportunity for self-paced retrieval did not change the fact that participants made more retrieval errors at transition points.
source: At the same time, the additional opportunity for self-paced retrieval did not change the fact that participants made more retrieval errors at transition points.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Individuals with low WM capacity showed larger chunk-boundary effects than individuals with high WM capacity.
source: Figure 2 also indicates that individuals with low WM capacity (i.e. determined through median split) showed larger chunk-boundary effects than individuals with high WM capacity.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The WM-group by chunk-boundary interaction was reliable across both experiments, F(1,56) = 6.63, MSE < 0.01, p = 0.01.
source: The WM-group by chunk-boundary interaction was reliable across both experiments, F(1,56) = 6.63, MSE < 0.01, p = 0.01
evidence: This is a specific statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: Oscillations centered around the alpha-frequency band showed sustained decoding of orientations, both late in the preparation period and early in the probe period.
source: Indeed, we found across Experiments 1 and 2 that oscillations centered around the alpha-frequency band showed sustained decoding of orientations, both late in the preparation period and early in the probe period (cluster-forming threshold p < 0.05, corrected significance level p < 0.001; Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data, with reference to Figure 3a.

claim: During the early probe period, the current element was also decoded from theta-band (4–7 Hz) activity.
source: In addition, during the early probe period, the current element was also decoded from theta-band (4–7 Hz) activity.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data.

claim: The finding that stimulus-evoked theta oscillations encoded spatial properties of visually presented stimulus is consistent with previous findings.
source: This result is consistent with previous findings in which stimulus-evoked theta oscillations encoded spatial properties of visually presented stimulus (Foster et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: During the probe period, decoding accuracy for elements in the alpha band predicted faster trial-to-trial responses over and above other constructs (i.e., within-chunk positions and chunk identity) in Experiment 1.
source: During the probe period, decoding accuracy for elements in the alpha band predicted faster trial-to-trial responses over and above other constructs (i.e., within-chunk positions and chunk identity), b = –032, SE = 0.09, t = –3.28, for Experiment 1
evidence: This is a specific finding from the multi-level modeling analysis.

claim: During the probe period, decoding accuracy for elements in the alpha band predicted faster trial-to-trial responses over and above other constructs (i.e., within-chunk positions and chunk identity) in Experiment 2.
source: and, b = –016, SE = 0.04, t = –3.51, for Experiment 2.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the multi-level modeling analysis.

claim: Within-chunk position information was present in a broader band of oscillations (4–16 Hz), but with a particular emphasis on the theta-band.
source: Across Experiments 1 and 2, our decoding results showed that within-chunk position information was present in a broader band of oscillations (4–16 Hz), but with a particular emphasis on the theta-band (cluster-forming threshold p < 0.05, corrected significance level p < 0.001; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data, with reference to Figure 3b.

claim: In the theta-band, robust decoding accuracy was observed at the beginning of the preparation and probe period.
source: In the theta-band, robust decoding accuracy was observed at the beginning of the preparation and probe period, whereas decoding accuracy gradually decreased in the alpha-band as the probe period approached.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data.

claim: Decoding accuracy gradually decreased in the alpha-band as the probe period approached.
source: In the theta-band, robust decoding accuracy was observed at the beginning of the preparation and probe period, whereas decoding accuracy gradually decreased in the alpha-band as the probe period approached.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data.

claim: For Experiment 1, more robust evidence for position information in the theta-band during the probe period predicted faster RTs, b = −0.011, SE = 0.0047, t = −2.44.
source: For Experiment 1, more robust evidence for position information in the theta-band during the probe period predicted faster RTs, b = −0.011, SE = 0.0047, t = −2.44.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the multi-level modeling analysis.

claim: Generalization accuracy for within-chunk position codes was essentially indistinguishable from reference scores, indicating that position codes were fairly independent from either specific elements or chunk positions.
source: In each case, generalization accuracy was essentially indistinguishable from reference scores, indicating that position codes were indeed fairly independent from either specific elements or chunk positions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the generalization analysis data presented in Table 1.

claim: Comparisons of average theta power at mid-frontal electrodes (Fz and Cz electrodes) between the first and the remaining two, within-chunk positions revealed no reliable differences for either the preparatory or the probe period in Experiment 1.
source: Comparisons of average theta power at mid-frontal electrodes (Fz and Cz electrodes) between the first and the remaining two, within-chunk positions revealed no reliable differences for either the preparatory or the probe period, t = 1.00, b = 0.49, SE = 0.49, and t = 0.17, b = 0.12, SE = 0.70, for Experiment 1
evidence: This is a specific finding from the analysis of theta power.

claim: Comparisons of average theta power at mid-frontal electrodes (Fz and Cz electrodes) between the first and the remaining two, within-chunk positions revealed no reliable differences for either the preparatory or the probe period in Experiment 2.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the analysis of theta power.

claim: Position decoding in the theta band does not simply reflect univariate and consistent changes across individuals that are solely driven by the modulation of frontal theta power.
source: These results indicate that position decoding in the theta band does not simply reflects univariate and consistent changes across individuals that are solely driven by the modulation of frontal theta power.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theta power analysis.

claim: The observed, position-decoding results are unlikely to be driven by a confound between positions and control/retrieval demands.
source: They also indicate that the observed, position-decoding results are unlikely to be driven by a confound between positions and control/retrieval demands.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theta power analysis.

claim: During the preparation period in both Experiments 1 and 2, position one was particularly distinct from positions 2 and 3, albeit with some remaining, numerical differences between positions 2 and 3.
source: As shown in Figure 4b, we found that for the preparation period in both Experiments 1 and 2, position one was particularly distinct, albeit with some remaining, numerical differences between positions 2 and 3.
evidence: This is an observation from the RSA analysis, with reference to Figure 4b.

claim: During the probe period, the three positions appeared to be equally dissimilar to each other.
source: However, during the probe period, the three positions appeared to be equally dissimilar to each other.
evidence: This is an observation from the RSA analysis.

claim: During the preparation period, only the unique-position-1 model significantly predicted the observed confusion matrix in Experiment 1.
source: During the preparation period, only the unique-position-1 model significantly predicted the observed confusion matrix (unique-position-1: b = 1.48, SE = 0.28, t = 5.36; discrete: b = -.10, SE = 0.16, t = -.59, for Experiment 1
evidence: This is a specific finding from the RSA regression analysis.

claim: During the preparation period, only the unique-position-1 model significantly predicted the observed confusion matrix in Experiment 2.
source: unique-position-1: b = 1.10, SE = 0.21, t = 5.16; discrete: b = 0.08, SE = 0.13, t = 0.67, for Experiment 2).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the RSA regression analysis.

claim: During the probe period, only the discrete model significantly predicted the observed pattern in Experiment 1.
source: However, only the discrete model significantly predicted the observed pattern during the probe period (unique-position-1: b = 0.21 SE = 0.29, t = 0.73; discrete: b = 0.75, SE = 0.23, t = 3.20, for Experiment 1
evidence: This is a specific finding from the RSA regression analysis.

claim: During the probe period, only the discrete model significantly predicted the observed pattern in Experiment 2.
source: unique-position-1: b = 0.16, SE = 0.36, t = 0.44; discrete: b = 1.01, SE = 0.30, t = 3.40, for Experiment 2).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the RSA regression analysis.

claim: The probe-period results suggest that theta-activity represents actual position codes.
source: Irrespective of the interpretation of results during the preparation period, the probe-period results suggest that theta-activity represents actual position codes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RSA analysis.

claim: The clear evidence of position coding during the probe period, but not the preparation period, is consistent with recent behavioral results indicating that people tend to update their current position within a larger sequence when they actually execute an individual, sequential element, not when they prepare for it.
source: The clear evidence of position coding during the probe period, but not the preparation period, is consistent with recent behavioral results indicating that people tend to update their current position within a larger sequence when they actually execute an individual, sequential element, not when they prepare for it (Mayr et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data and supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In no case did we find any indication of a forward predictability pattern during the time- and frequency-ranges that contained robust element information in Experiment 1.
source: In no case did we find any indication of a forward predictability pattern during the time- and frequency-ranges that contained robust element information (preparation period/alpha band: t(30) = 0.739, p = 0.465, probe period/alpha band: t(30) = -1.60, p = 0.120, probe period/theta band: t(30) = -1.26, p = 0.218, for Experiment 1
evidence: This is a specific finding from the associative chaining analysis.

claim: In no case did we find any indication of a forward predictability pattern during the time- and frequency-ranges that contained robust element information in Experiment 2.
source: preparation period/alpha band: t(30) = 1.07, p = 0.293, probe period/alpha band: t(30) = 0.912, p = 0.369, probe period/theta band: t(30) = 0.425, p = 0.674, for Experiment 2).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the associative chaining analysis.

claim: The results are consistent with the conclusion that chaining was not a major factor in the current paradigm.
source: Nevertheless, they are consistent with the conclusion that chaining was not a major factor in the current paradigm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the associative chaining analysis.

claim: Information about the identity of chunks was decodable during the preparation period.
source: We found that information about the identity of chunks was decodable during the preparation period (cluster-forming threshold p < 0.05, corrected significance level p < 0.05; Figure 5).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: Across both Experiments 1 and 2, the chunk identity decoding effect was most sustained 600 ms prior to the onset of the test probe in the alpha-band (8–12 Hz).
source: Across both Experiments 1 and 2, the effect was most sustained 600 ms prior to the onset of the test probe in the alpha-band (8–12 Hz).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data.

claim: Only very little chunk-identity information was detectable during the probe period.
source: Generally, only very little chunk-identity information was detectable during the probe period.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data.

claim: There is no evidence that chunk information is present only for position 1.
source: As evident in the Figure 6, while there is some variability in the strength of expression of chunk information for positions 2 and 3 across the two experiments, there is no evidence that chunk information is present only for position 1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of chunk information across positions, with reference to Figure 6.

claim: A contrast between positions 1 versus positions 2 and 3 produced no significant effect in Experiment 1 or Experiment 2.
source: A contrast between positions 1 versus positions 2 and 3 produced a significant effect in neither experiment, Experiment 1: t(30) = .02, p = 0.99, Experiment 2: t(30) = .88, p = 0.38.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: Information about the current chunk is represented not only when a new chunk needs to be accessed, but at least to some degree also while within-chunk elements are being processed.
